newsitem.title: USA: NYMEX chairman says regulatory relief inevitable.
newsitem.headline: NYMEX chairman says regulatory relief inevitable.

text.p: Inevitable changes to commodity regulations will help NYMEX compete better against London Metal Exchange copper futures, make it easier to launch new contracts and reduce the chances of a Sumitomo-type scandal recurring, said NYMEX chairman Daniel Rappaport.

As London prepared for its first post-Sumitomo debacle LME Week, Rappaport said he was reasonably happy with NYMEX's COMEX division copper futures contract. Open interest was up 20 percent and volume up 15 percent this year.
COMEX governors on Tuesday discussed introducing large-order trading to boost volumes further. Calendar strip trading was introduced on September 20.

"But there is no one thing that will turn this thing round. What we really need is some regulatory relief to be creative to compete against over-the-counter markets and foreign exchanges," Rappaport told Reuters.
Three bills to ease regulations in the 1972 Commodity Exchange Act have been introduced in past few months.

None will be enacted as the 104th Congress has drawn to a pre-election close. So far the Commodity Futures Trading Commission says it has enough powers to survey markets and take action, but officials said they were still reviewing the bills.

"The CFTC fears any action - they prefer no changes at all, but we have crossed that hurdle," Rappaport said. "Congress has recognised that the CFTC is wrong and that some legislative changes must be made."
The bills included provisions giving regulatory powers over foreign based commodity contracts with physical delivery in the U.S.
"The House bill does not go far enough but it's a good start to the extent if passed, it will open the door and begin to address some of the issues that have been neglected," Rappaport said.

He preferred the bill put forward by Rep Charles Schumer because it was more focused and insisted that foreign contracts physically delivered in the U.S. come under the same rules as domestic contracts.
Foreign exchanges conducting trade in the U.S. should play by U.S. rules or go home, Rappaport said. "This principle applies across the commercial spectrum, not just commodities."
The LME opened warehouses in the U.S. for its copper contract in April 1995. The trade widely believed that most of of copper stored in Long Beach was held by Sumitomo Corp.
"We were getting requests and having some concerns of our own about anomalies in the market as a result of, let's say unusual accummulation of stocks in the LME warehouses," Rappaport said.
"We we were unable to get any information. The CFTC was unable to get information as to who was holding those stocks and what their intent was. This is unacceptable."
The LME warehouses made a mockery of COMEX's limits on how big a position could be held on the New York exchange, Rappaport said, and made it difficult to launch new contracts.

"Unless we get some regulatory relief, I don't believe there is any possibility of competing with the LME on an aluminum contract even though the U.S. is the largest producer and consumer of aluminum," Rappaport said. "But if we get regulatory relief then we will launch a contract."

NYMEX president Patrick Thompson, on a recent visit to Asia, was asked to consider launching an Asian-deliverable copper contract, Rappaport said. "There was a lot of dissatisfaction following the Sumitomo scandal with the LME copper contract."

He added there was a need for a contract that tracked Asian copper supply and demand more closely than LME did, but without offending COMEX's "loyal and dedicated constituency" in the U.S. where it is the main pricing reference.
"We don't have the answer yet," Rappaport said.
